Marked improvements have occurred in the outcome and reliability of liver transplan- tation and it is now seen as standard therapy for acute and chronic hepatic failure, regardless of aetiology,1-3 and some metabolic disorders.4 The 1-year patient and graft survival rates2,4,5 are about 90%. The liver induces some tolerance and liver transplant re- cipients usually require less immunosuppression than oth- er solid organ transplant patients.6 Immunosuppressive regimens generally combine a calcineurin inhibitor (ciclosporin or tacrolimus) with a corticosteroid and aza- thioprine or mycophenolate mofetil; such triple therapy prevents acute rejection episodes in the majority of cas- es.7-9 Double therapy with ciclosporin or tacrolimus and corticosteroids is also used,8,10 and monotherapy with a calcineurin inhibitor alone has also been used, allowing for complete corticosteroid withdrawal or avoidance.10 A review of corticosteroid-free strategies in liver trans- plantation concluded that up to 50% of patients can avoid corticosteroids with little modification of their mainte- nance immunosuppressive regimen; adding mycopheno- late mofetil and/or induction therapy with antibodies can increase this percentage, although over-immunosuppres- sion may be a problem.
